explanation: The nucleus ambiguus is the common motor nucleus for cranial nerves IX, X, and XI. It gives rise to special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) fibers that supply pharyngeal arch muscles (stylopharyngeus via IX, pharyngeal/laryngeal muscles via X, sternocleidomastoid and trapezius via XI).

The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is the only nucleus in the CNS that contains pseudounipolar sensory neuron cell bodies. It carries proprioceptive impulses from muscles of mastication and other structures, making it a General Somatic Afferent (GSA) nucleus.
The parasympathetic nucleus of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is the inferior salivatory nucleus. It provides parasympathetic preganglionic fibers to the parotid gland via the otic ganglion.

The thyrohyoid muscle is supplied by C1 spinal nerve fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) as the nerve to thyrohyoid. This is an exception to the rule that infrahyoid muscles are supplied by ansa cervicalis.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies the mucous membrane of the oropharynx, including the palatine tonsils and posterior one-third of the tongue. The nasopharynx is supplied by the maxillary nerve (V2) via the sphenopalatine ganglion.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides the parasympathetic and motor fibers to the nucleus ambiguus for innervation of the stylopharyngeus muscle. The nucleus ambiguus also receives contributions from CN X and XI.

Sodium (Na+) is the primary ion responsible for rapid depolarization during the upstroke of the action potential. Na+ channels open rapidly causing an influx of Na+, creating the spike. K+ is responsible for repolarization during the downstroke.
